commitResults.messageTitle: Level-0: greet the user and exit
commitResults.messageBody:
Print a greeting and a farewell, each separated by a horizontal
divider, so the program satisfies the Level-0 requirement of
greeting the user and exiting.

Extract the divider and the ASCII-art banner into named constants
so the 60-character divider literal is defined once rather than
repeated at each of its three uses.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add a save-file representation to the Task hierarchy
commitResults.messageBody:
Give Task a toFileFormat() that renders the fields every task shares,
and have each subclass prepend its type letter and append its own
fields, mirroring how toString() is already built up.

Keep the save-file completion flag (getStatusFlag) separate from the
on-screen icon (getStatusIcon) so the display can be changed later
without invalidating files that have already been written.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add a Storage class for reading and writing the task file
commitResults.messageBody:
Build the path from relative parts with Paths.get so it works from
whatever directory the program is run in and uses the separator the
host OS expects, rather than a hard-coded absolute path.

Treat a missing file or folder as an empty list rather than an error,
so the chatbot runs on a computer that has never run it before, and
create the folder on demand when saving.

Skip lines that do not match the expected format instead of letting a
corrupted file stop the load, reporting how many were dropped so the
user knows their list is incomplete.

commitResults.messageTitle: Level-7: load tasks at startup and save on every change
commitResults.messageBody:
Read the saved tasks before the command loop starts, and rewrite the
file after any command that changes the list. "list" is excluded, so
reading the list does not rewrite the file for nothing.

Report load warnings once at startup rather than staying silent, so a
user whose save file was partly unreadable finds out before they start
adding to it. A failed save is reported too and leaves the session
running, since the in-memory list is still correct.

Ignore /data/ so a user's own task file is not committed.

Add saving to and loading from the hard disk (Level-7): a Storage
class that reads and writes ./data/milo.txt using a relative,
OS-independent path, tolerates a missing file or folder on first run,
and skips unreadable lines rather than failing the whole load.

Move every System.out / Scanner interaction out of Milo and into a
new Ui class: the banner and greeting, the divider-framed response
block, load-status and error reporting, and command reading. Milo now
talks to the user only through ui.*, never through System.out/in
directly.

Behaviour is unchanged: the fixed regression scenario produces
byte-identical output before and after this commit.

Wrap the task ArrayList in a TaskList that owns add/delete/get/size
and the numbered-lines rendering that used to be Milo's formatTasks.
Bounds checking (delete/get) now lives with the list itself rather
than being the caller's responsibility.

Milo's list-shaped helpers (parseTaskIndex, setDone, deleteTask) now
take a TaskList instead of a raw ArrayList<Task>; the number-parsing
and user-phrased error messages stay in Milo for now since they are
about interpreting user text, not about the list itself.

Behaviour is unchanged: the fixed regression scenario produces
byte-identical output before and after this commit.

Bring in Gradle build support from the SE-EDU Duke template repo:
build.gradle, the Gradle wrapper (gradlew/gradlew.bat), and the
wrapper's properties/jar. This only added files relative to where
the branch diverged (befbd32), so it merges cleanly against all the
work done since then.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add seedu-git-standard skill and AGENTS.md rule
commitResults.messageBody:
Commit messages and branch names so far followed no documented
convention beyond "explain the rationale" and "use lightweight
tags". Let's codify the SE-EDU git conventions (imperative subject
line, 50/72 character limits, what-and-why commit bodies, kebab-case
branch names, one logical change per commit) as a project skill, and
point AGENTS.md at it so future commits and branches follow it
without having to be reminded each time.

commitResults.messageTitle: Ui: import List instead of using it fully-qualified
commitResults.messageBody:
showLoadStatus() took its warnings parameter as java.util.List<String>
written out in full, instead of importing java.util.List and using
the simple name like every other type in the codebase does. The
SE-EDU coding standard being adopted in this project bans inline
fully-qualified type names in favour of an explicit import, so let's
bring this one method in line with the rest of the class.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add seedu-java-coding-standard skill and AGENTS.md rule
commitResults.messageBody:
The project had no documented Java style beyond a couple of scattered
Javadoc/simplicity notes, so consistency depended on whoever wrote
each file. Let's codify the SE-EDU intermediate Java conventions
(naming, layout, import ordering, Javadoc) as a project skill, and
point AGENTS.md at it so it gets applied automatically to code written
or reviewed here from now on, rather than needing to be restated per
change.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add find command to search tasks by keyword
Fix switch-indentation guidance in the coding-standard skill
Add a JavaFX GUI for Milo
Fix GUI bugs and add proper styling

commitResults.messageBody:
Several methods depend on conditions that their callers have already
established. Parser only routes the three add-type command words into
buildTask, resolveTaskIndex range-checks a number before handing the
index on, requireInRange rules out the one case where a removal could
come back with nothing, and both Parser and Storage reject an empty
description before a Task is ever constructed. None of that is stated
where the dependent code sits, so a change that breaks one of these
surfaces later and elsewhere, as an out-of-range index or a save file
that has quietly lost a task.

Let's record each assumption as an assertion at the point that relies on
it, with a comment saying which caller guarantees it. An assertion that
fails names the broken assumption at the line that depended on it,
instead of leaving a downstream symptom to be traced back.

These cover internal invariants only. User input stays the job of
MiloException, because the JVM disables assertions unless -ea is passed:
an input check written as an assertion would be absent from the shipped
JAR, which is exactly where it would be needed. Gradle's test and run
tasks enable assertions by default, so they take effect during
development without any build change.

commitResults.messageTitle: Ignore whitespace-only input in the GUI
commitResults.messageBody:
The send handler drops input only when the text field is exactly empty.
Typing a few spaces and pressing Enter passes them to the parser, which
splits them into an empty command word and answers 'I don't know what ""
means'. The user is told their input was an unrecognised command when
they have, as far as they can tell, sent nothing at all.

Let's treat a field holding only whitespace the same way an empty one is
already treated, and return without sending it. A blank line carries no
command, so the parser has nothing useful to do with it either way.

Guarding at the point of entry keeps the parser free of a special case
that exists only because one interface allows the input through.

commitResults.messageTitle: Milo: stop shadowing the isExit field in run()
commitResults.messageBody:
run() declares a local isExit that hides the field of the same name. The
two are never the same variable: run() reads and writes the local, while
getResponse() and isExit() read and write the field. A reader has to work
out which of the two any given line refers to, and a later change that
moves code between the loop and the field's accessors would silently
target the wrong one.

Let's delete the local and let run() use the field, which already starts
out false and already means exactly what the loop wants it to mean.

The two entry points now agree on where the session's exit state lives,
so there is one answer to "has Milo been told to stop" rather than one
per method.

getDisplayLines and getMatchingDisplayLines differ only in which tasks
they render, what the header says, and what to show when there is nothing
to show. The numbering itself, the off-by-one between the user's 1-based
numbers and the list's 0-based indices, and the sizing of the array are
written out twice, so a fix to the numbering has to be found and made in
both places.

Let's pull the shared rendering into one private helper that takes the
tasks, the header and the empty-case message, and let both public methods
supply those three things.

The helper takes a List rather than the field, so the search path can pass
its filtered tasks through the same code as the full list instead of
keeping a parallel copy of the numbering logic.

commitResults.messageTitle: Parser: split buildTask into one builder per task type
commitResults.messageBody:
buildTask reads the command word and then, inside a single switch, does
the whole job of each task type: locating markers, slicing the arguments
around them, checking each resulting piece, and phrasing an error for
every way the input can fall short. The method mixes one high-level
decision with three low-level procedures, so a reader after the deadline
rules has to scroll past the event rules to be sure they have them all,
and the two "description is empty" checks sit far enough apart to read
as unrelated.

Let's give each task type its own private builder and leave buildTask
with only the decision of which one to call. Each builder is then short
enough to read in one go, and the switch states the routing rules on
their own.

The builders stay private and keep returning Task, so this changes how
the parsing reads rather than what any caller can do with it.

commitResults.messageTitle: TaskList: build the display lines with streams
commitResults.messageBody:
Both display methods allocate an array of the right size, write the
header into slot zero, and then fill the rest with a counter that has to
be offset by one against the loop index. The offset is the interesting
part of the code and it is the part most easily got wrong, but it is
buried among the bookkeeping the array demands. The search path adds a
second loop whose only job is to copy matching tasks into a list before
that rendering can start.

Let's express both as streams: a filter for the search, and a range
mapped to numbered lines concatenated after the header. The numbering
stays visible as the one expression that produces a line, and the
array is built at the end by toArray rather than sized up front.

Streams suit this because each method is a pipeline that reads tasks
and produces lines without changing anything along the way.

commitResults.messageTitle: Storage: read and write the save file with streams
commitResults.messageBody:
Saving walks the tasks and appends each formatted line to a list that was
created empty a line earlier, which is three statements to say that the
saved lines are the tasks mapped through toFileFormat. Loading is harder
to follow: one loop trims a line, skips it if blank, parses it, and keeps
a running count of the failures, so four separate concerns share one body
and the skipped counter has to be maintained by hand.

Let's express both as pipelines. Saving becomes a map over the tasks.
Loading first reduces the file to its non-blank lines, then maps those
through a parse that yields an empty result for a line it cannot read, so
the count of skipped lines falls out of the difference in sizes rather
than being tracked separately.

parseTask throws a checked exception, which a stream cannot carry, so a
small wrapper turns that into an Optional at the boundary. The wrapper is
where the decision to tolerate a bad line now lives, which is a better
home for it than the middle of a loop.
